questions.q: What does REINFORCE use as its estimate of Q^pi(s, a) in the policy gradient theorem?
options: A separately trained neural network critic
The actual Monte Carlo return G_t observed from that timestep to the end of the episode
The maximum reward ever seen in training
A fixed constant set before training begins
questions.explain: REINFORCE substitutes the actual sampled return-to-go, G_t, for Q^pi(s,a), making it a pure Monte Carlo policy gradient method with no learned value function.

questions.q: What is the REINFORCE parameter update rule?
options: theta <- theta + alpha * grad_theta log(pi_theta(a_t|s_t)) * G_t
theta <- theta - alpha * Q(s,a)
theta <- theta * gamma
theta <- theta + alpha * reward_t only, ignoring future rewards
questions.explain: REINFORCE applies the policy gradient theorem with G_t standing in for Q^pi(s,a): theta is updated by the gradient of the log-probability of the taken action, scaled by that return-to-go.

questions.q: Why is computing returns backward through an episode (G_t = r_t + gamma * G_(t+1)) preferred over summing forward from each timestep?
options: It produces a different, more correct answer
It computes all returns in a single linear-time pass instead of a quadratic-time one
It removes the need for a discount factor
It only works for episodes of length 1
questions.explain: Summing forward from every timestep to the end is O(T^2); computing backward reuses the already-computed G_(t+1), making it O(T).

questions.q: Why does the REINFORCE training loop negate the policy gradient objective before calling .backward()?
options: Because rewards must always be negative
Because PyTorch optimizers perform gradient descent (minimization), while the policy gradient is an ascent rule on expected return
Because the discount factor is negative
It's a bug and should not be done
questions.explain: The policy gradient theorem is inherently a gradient ascent rule. Since PyTorch optimizers minimize a loss, the objective is negated so that minimizing the loss corresponds to ascending the true policy gradient objective.

questions.q: Why does REINFORCE have high variance?
options: Because it never uses a discount factor
Because G_t is a single sample from one trajectory, and identical early states can lead to very different sampled returns due to later randomness
Because the policy network has too few layers
Because it always converges to the same answer every episode
questions.explain: G_t reflects only one particular rollout of the policy's stochastic action choices and the environment's randomness, so it can vary a great deal between episodes even from the same starting state.
